questions.prompt: You want more of the scene in focus, from the near object to the far one. Which aperture change helps?
choices: Opening the iris, such as F8 to F4
Closing the iris, such as F4 to F8
questions.explanation: A smaller opening gives more depth of field. Going from F4.0 to F5.6 makes the picture darker with more of the scene in focus.

questions.prompt: A wide-open iris (a low f-number) tends to give…
choices: More light and a shallower depth of field
Less light and a deeper depth of field
questions.explanation: The bigger the opening, the more light, and the less of the scene stays in focus.

questions.prompt: You close the iris for more depth of field in a dim room, and the picture gets too dark. What can you do to brighten it?
choices: Raise the gain or slow the shutter, accepting more noise or more motion blur
questions.explanation: Brightness has to come from somewhere. Gain costs noise, and a slower shutter costs motion blur.

questions.prompt: What is the house default in the Portable Cameras activity?
choices: F4.0, 3 dB (ISO 400 on the GH5), 1/60, 3200 K, autofocus
questions.explanation: The house default is the known baseline: F4.0 · 3 dB (ISO 400 on the GH5) · 1/60 · 3200 K · autofocus.

questions.prompt: When do you set a camera to the house default in the Cameras activity?
choices: Never, you leave it as you found it
At the start, and again before the camera goes back in the cabinet
questions.explanation: You set it twice: once to start from a known baseline, and once so the next person finds it that way.

questions.prompt: A camera comes out of the cabinet in whatever state the last person left it. What do you do before recording?
choices: Set it to a known baseline and confirm all five values on the display
Start recording and fix it afterward
Leave it, because the last person set it up
questions.explanation: Nobody is going to walk you through the menus. Set the five values and read them off the screen before you record.

questions.prompt: After you record your first clip, what should you do before shooting the others?
choices: Keep shooting and check at the end
Pull the SD card, open the file on a computer, and confirm it plays and has audio
questions.explanation: Do not shoot the other clips before you know the card is actually recording. Students lose whole sessions this way.

questions.prompt: When comparing what a setting does, why change only one setting at a time and keep the framing identical?
choices: Otherwise you can’t tell what caused the difference
The camera can only store one setting
questions.explanation: If the framing, the light, or two settings changed, the comparison is worthless.

questions.prompt: The camera says the SD card is full, locked, or missing. What should you NOT do?
choices: Check that the card is seated
Find a different card or ask
questions.explanation: Do not reformat. Check the card is seated and the slider is up, then find a different card or ask.

questions.prompt: In the Cameras activity, what is a “slate”?
choices: Reading your settings aloud on camera
questions.explanation: Reading the settings out loud on camera records which values each clip used, so you can match clips to settings later.

questions.prompt: What does an ND (neutral density) filter do?
choices: Reduces the light reaching the sensor without changing the color
questions.explanation: Neutral means it dims the picture without tinting it.

questions.prompt: It’s bright daylight. You want a wide-open iris and 1/60 shutter, but the shot is overexposed. What helps?
questions.explanation: The ND filter takes light away so you can keep the aperture and shutter speed you actually want.

questions.prompt: Why use an ND filter instead of just closing the iris?
choices: An ND filter makes the shot sharper
ND filters change the white balance for you
Closing the iris would change your depth of field, and an ND filter doesn’t
questions.explanation: With ND you can keep the depth of field and motion blur you chose and still control brightness.

questions.prompt: It’s a dark recital hall. Will an ND filter help you get a brighter picture?
choices: No, an ND filter only removes light
Only if the shutter is slow
questions.explanation: ND filters are for too much light. In a dark hall you need the opposite.

questions.prompt: An ND filter cuts the light by 3 stops. What fraction of the light gets through?
questions.explanation: Each stop halves the light, so three stops is one half times one half times one half, which is one eighth.

questions.prompt: Focal length, in millimeters, mainly describes what about a lens?
choices: How much light it lets in
How wide or narrow (zoomed in) a view it gives
How close the subject must be
questions.explanation: A shorter focal length gives a wider view. A longer one is more zoomed in.

questions.prompt: You zoom in to fill the frame with a soloist. What changed?
choices: The focal length got longer, so the field of view is narrower
questions.explanation: Zooming in raises the focal length and narrows what the camera sees.

questions.prompt: Which of these focal lengths gives the widest view?
questions.explanation: The shorter the focal length, the wider the view.

questions.prompt: You need to fit a whole ensemble in the shot, and you can’t move the camera back. What helps?
questions.explanation: Zooming out gives a wider view. At a recital, wide framing also leaves room for performers when they bow.

questions.prompt: What is focus distance?
choices: How far the camera can zoom
How much of the scene is sharp
The distance from the camera to the thing that is in sharp focus
questions.explanation: It’s where the lens is set to be sharp. Depth of field is how far the sharp zone extends from there.

questions.prompt: A camera is on manual focus, set on a singer. The singer walks well forward. What happens?
choices: They stay sharp, because focus follows people
They go soft, because they’re no longer at the distance the lens is set to
questions.explanation: In manual focus the focus distance stays where you left it, so check focus whenever the subject moves.

questions.prompt: You refocus from a near object to a far one. What did you change?
questions.explanation: Refocusing changes the distance the lens is sharp at. Focal length is how wide the view is.

questions.prompt: What does “AoIP” stand for?
questions.explanation: Dante is audio over IP: multichannel digital audio over a network.

questions.prompt: What can a single Ethernet cable do on a Dante network?
choices: Carry many channels of audio, replacing a thick analog snake
Carry audio but never at full quality
questions.explanation: Instead of a thick analog snake with oodles of cables, there is one Ethernet cable.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Dante Virtual Soundcard (DVS) is true?
choices: It only works with one DAW
It’s licensed software that makes your computer appear as an audio interface in a DAW’s I/O
questions.explanation: Any DAW (Logic, Ableton, Reaper) can use DVS if it’s installed. Choose the correct audio I/O in the DAW.

questions.prompt: In Dante, what do TX and RX stand for?
questions.explanation: TX is transmit and RX is receive.

questions.prompt: Dante Controller “does not make sound.” What does it do?
choices: It plays audio over the network
It creates the subscription between transmit and receive channels, like a virtual patch bay across the network
questions.explanation: It is the routing tool: it decides where network audio goes. The sound itself comes from the DAW through DVS.

questions.prompt: Where do you choose which audio interface a DAW uses?
choices: In the Dante routing matrix only
In the DAW’s audio I/O settings
questions.explanation: DAW I/O is where you choose the audio interface. Dante Controller chooses where network audio goes.

questions.prompt: Which tool chooses which transmit channel feeds which receive channel on the network?
questions.explanation: Dante Controller creates the subscriptions. It does not choose the DAW’s device.

questions.prompt: To send audio from a DAW out over Dante, what should the DAW’s output device be set to?
choices: Whatever the other computer is using
questions.explanation: The transmitting DAW’s output has to go to DVS, or nothing reaches the network.

questions.prompt: On the receiving computer, how do you hear and record the incoming Dante audio?
choices: Set the DAW’s input to Dante Virtual Soundcard, make a track with input Dante 1–2, and turn on input monitoring
Set the output to Dante Virtual Soundcard
Nothing is needed once routing is green
questions.explanation: The receiving track needs its input set to the right Dante channels, and input monitoring on so you can hear it.

questions.prompt: Dante Controller shows green routing, but a classmate hears nothing. What’s the most likely next thing to check?
choices: Whether their DAW’s input device is actually set to Dante Virtual Soundcard
questions.explanation: Green routing means the network connection exists. The DAW still has to be listening to DVS.

questions.prompt: To send a stereo signal from one computer to another, which routes do you make in Dante Controller?
choices: Only transmit ch. 1 to receive ch. 1
Transmit ch. 1 to receive ch. 2 only
No routes: DVS does it automatically
Transmit ch. 1 to receive ch. 1, and transmit ch. 2 to receive ch. 2
questions.explanation: Stereo is two channels, so both must be routed.

questions.prompt: You hear sound in only one ear when you expected stereo. What’s the most likely cause?
choices: The track is mono instead of stereo, or only one Dante channel got routed
Dante Controller needs to be reinstalled
questions.explanation: Check that the source is actually stereo and that both Dante channels 1 and 2 are routed.

questions.prompt: In Dante Controller, what should the routing squares look like once a route is made?
questions.explanation: Green means connected. Gray or red means something isn’t.

questions.prompt: How do you tell your computer from others in Dante Controller?
choices: By its IP address written on the monitor
By the color of the squares
By its Local Hostname (the iMac number), typed into the Filter boxes
questions.explanation: Note the Local Hostname in System Settings, then use Filter Transmitters and Filter Receivers to find it.

questions.prompt: Why build a Multi-Output Device on the transmitting computer in a Dante computer to computer situation?
choices: To receive audio from the network
So it can send audio over Dante and still hear it locally
questions.explanation: The Multi-Output Device combines Dante Virtual Soundcard with your local headphone output.

questions.prompt: If you’re connecting two computers with Dante and you want the transmitter to be able to “hear itself”, you’ll open Audio MIDI Setup. After building a Multi-Output Device, what should the DAW’s output be set to?
questions.explanation: The Multi-Output Device is what sends to both places at once.

questions.prompt: In Audio MIDI Setup, in a Multi-Output Device, what determines each device’s channel numbering?
choices: The order you check the boxes
Every device always starts at channel 1
questions.explanation: Channel numbering follows the order of the checked boxes.

questions.prompt: When you build a Multi-Output Device, which box do you check first?
questions.explanation: Check the DVS box before the local interface, or your channel numbering will come out different than expected.

questions.prompt: Three computers each send a stereo source to one receiving computer. Which channel map avoids collisions?
choices: It doesn’t matter, Dante mixes them
Transmitter 1 to channels 1–2, transmitter 2 to 3–4, transmitter 3 to 5–6
questions.explanation: Each source needs its own receive channel pair so each lands on its own track.

questions.prompt: Why does each transmitter need its own receive channel pair?
choices: So each source arrives on a separate track instead of overriding another
Dante limits the whole network to 2 channels
questions.explanation: Dante doesn’t mix two sources into one destination.

questions.prompt: You route a second source to a channel pair that’s already in use. What happens?
choices: The new route silently overrides the first one: Dante doesn’t mix them
Dante refuses and shows an error
questions.explanation: Dante never lets two sources share one destination. The first source just stops arriving.

questions.prompt: In Dante: You only hear Transmitter 2, and Transmitter 1 should also be playing. What’s the most likely cause?
choices: The receiving computer needs more RAM
Both were routed to the same receive channel pair, so Transmitter 2 overrode Transmitter 1
DVS supports only one transmitter at a time
questions.explanation: Look at the full routing matrix, not just your own row.

questions.prompt: In the Dante Jam Session, which computer acts as the “mixer” of the multiple software instruments on other computers?
choices: The receiving computer, whose output would feed the room’s speakers
questions.explanation: Everyone’s audio routes into one computer that acts as the mixer. That computer’s output is what feeds the room.

questions.prompt: How is the Dante Jam Session different from Dante Broadcast?
choices: In the jam, many senders go to one receiver; in Broadcast, one computer sends to one or more computers
Broadcast uses many senders and one receiver
questions.explanation: Broadcast is one computer to one or more computers. The jam session is many senders into one receiver.

questions.prompt: The receiving computer hears nothing. What do you check first in Dante Controller?
choices: Whether the computer is plugged into AC
Whether the routing squares are green or gray/red
The color of the Ethernet cable
questions.explanation: Start with the network connection. Then check the DAWs’ DVS settings, input monitoring, and the headphones.

questions.prompt: Dante Controller shows a red square in the lower right, such as “Clock: No clock source found.” What does it mean?
choices: A network-wide clock problem: a master clock source needs to be set and active
questions.explanation: This is a network-wide problem, not just your computer. Flag it to your instructor if you can’t resolve it.

questions.prompt: In OH B01, which device must you NOT re-route or disconnect in Dante Controller?
choices: Any other iMac in the room
The receiving computer in a jam session
The one labeled INST, the instructor computer feeding the room’s main speakers
questions.explanation: Breaking INST cuts the sound for the whole room, including other classes.

questions.prompt: In the DAW to X32 example, what connects the DAW DVS transmit channels to the X32’s receive channels?
choices: A subscription made in Dante Controller
questions.explanation: DAW to DVS to the Dante network, then Dante Controller subscribes transmit to receive, and the X32 Dante card receives.

questions.prompt: Multitrack DAW outputs 1–8 are sent over Dante to an X32 with a correctly configured Dante expansion card installed. What does each output end up as?
choices: Its own channel on the X32, on its own fader
questions.explanation: If the routing works, each stem lands on its own X32 fader.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct signal path for sending DAW audio to another computer over Dante?
choices: DAW, then the network, then the other computer’s speakers directly
DVS, then the DAW, then Dante Controller, then the network
DAW, then DVS, then the network, then DVS, then the other DAW, then its output
Network, then DAW, then DVS, then Dante Controller
questions.explanation: The activities’ diagram: source to DAW to DVS to network to DVS to DAW to output.

questions.prompt: On an XLR or other connector, which gender has the pins that stick out?
questions.explanation: Male connectors have the pins (or the plug part); female connectors have the holes (or the socket).

questions.prompt: A microphone has a male XLR connector. Which end of an XLR cable goes onto the microphone?
choices: Either end, because XLR has no gender
questions.explanation: A male connector needs a female one to mate with it, so the cable’s female end plugs onto the mic. The male end goes into the mixer or interface.

questions.prompt: An XLR input jack on a mixer or audio interface is normally which gender?
choices: Neither; XLR inputs have no gender
questions.explanation: Inputs are normally female, which is why the cable’s male end goes into them. (A combo jack takes either XLR or ¼-inch, but its XLR part is still female.)

questions.prompt: You need a longer XLR run and want to join two XLR cables. How do they connect?
choices: The male end of one into the female end of the other
Male to male, with a gender changer
Female to female, with a gender changer
They can’t be joined; you need one longer cable
questions.explanation: Each cable has one male end and one female end, so they chain end to end: male into female.

questions.prompt: How should you describe a cable to someone who needs to find it?
choices: By both ends: the connector and gender at each, like “XLR female to ¼-inch TRS”
By what it’s usually used for, like “mic cable”
By the brand name on the jacket
questions.explanation: A cable is defined by its two ends. Color, length, and nickname don’t tell the person which one to fetch.

questions.prompt: Put the three HDMI sizes in order, largest connector to smallest.
questions.explanation: Full-size HDMI is the standard plug; mini is smaller; micro is the smallest of the three.

questions.prompt: An SDI video cable ends in which kind of connector?
questions.explanation: SDI uses BNC connectors: round, with a twist-lock collar.

questions.prompt: A camera’s HDMI output is a micro HDMI port, and the monitor’s input is a full-size HDMI port. Which cable do you need?
choices: SDI with BNC on both ends
questions.explanation: The cable has to match the port at each end: micro at the camera, full-size at the monitor.

questions.prompt: A 3.5 mm to dual RCA cable ends in two RCA plugs. Why two?
choices: One carries the left channel and one the right
One carries signal and one carries power
One is audio and one is video
questions.explanation: The 3.5 mm stereo plug carries left and right; the cable splits them onto two RCA plugs, one per channel.

questions.prompt: A gig is in Salmon. What does that tell you about the services it needs?
choices: Standard A/V recording only, since that’s Salmon’s system
Not enough: recording, livestream, FOH, or a mix
FOH only, since Salmon has its own PA system
A livestream only, since Salmon is set up to stream
questions.explanation: A venue doesn’t automatically determine the service. Salmon gigs can involve recording, livestreaming, FOH, or a combination.

questions.prompt: Chapman Auditorium and Memorial Hall are…
choices: Two halls on opposite sides of campus
questions.explanation: Chapman Auditorium and Memorial Hall are the same venue, and it uses the Standard Gear Kit workflow.

questions.prompt: A concert in Memorial Hall or Fish Chapel usually uses which workflow?
choices: The Musco multicam workflow, with a crew
Salmon’s built-in A/V and livestream system
questions.explanation: Memorial Hall, Fish Chapel, and similar spaces use the Standard Gear Kit: portable audio, portable cameras, and maybe a board feed.

questions.prompt: Chapman on Broadway (COB) borrows a portable PA for a show. Do we officially staff it with recording engineers?
choices: Yes, always with at least two engineers
Yes, but only to run FOH for the show
Only if the show is going to be livestreamed
No: it’s student-run, though we share gear
questions.explanation: COB and CSOP are student-run productions. We don’t officially staff them, but we often share our gear with them.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a typical Salmon FOH gig?
choices: A search recording in a classroom
questions.explanation: Salmon FOH gigs include Mariachi, Commercial Music Ensemble, Vocal Jazz, and sometimes Music at Noon. Wassail is at Musco.

questions.prompt: Which ensemble’s concerts are a typical Musco gig?
questions.explanation: Musco gigs include TCO, Wind Symphony, the choral ensembles, Wassail, Sholund, and other large events.

questions.prompt: What’s the goal for every student who passes MUS 248?
choices: Specialize early in one gig family
Be capable across every normal gig type
Run a Musco gig without needing a crew
questions.explanation: The goal is universal qualification, not early specialization. Students will have different strengths, but everyone needs the core skills.

questions.prompt: What’s the right attire for a gig?
choices: Anything comfortable, since you’re behind the scenes
A Chapman logo shirt, so staff know who you are
Closed-toed shoes, no logos, and all black at Musco
All black at Salmon; anything goes at Musco
questions.explanation: Closed-toed shoes and no logos on shirts, always. At Musco, all black.

questions.prompt: When should you ask about anything that depends on house staff, lighting, performers, or venue access?
choices: Early, as soon as you can
questions.explanation: Other people’s time is the bottleneck. Ask early so there’s time to adjust the plan around their answers.

questions.prompt: Something goes wrong during the performance. What does “protect the performance” mean?
choices: Stop the concert so it can be fixed properly
Walk onstage right away to fix the mic
Solve it quietly without disrupting the event
Announce the problem so the audience understands
questions.explanation: Stay quiet, stay organized, and solve problems without disrupting the event.

questions.prompt: Which list matches “after the gig”?
choices: Power down, transfer and verify media, return gear ready
Return the gear and let the next engineer check it over
Wipe the cards right away so they’re ready next time
Leave the media on the cards for whoever goes next
questions.explanation: Stop and power down what you used, transfer and verify the media, and return gear ready for the next engineer.

questions.prompt: Before your gig, you find another engineer’s data transfer that was started but never finished. What do you do?
choices: Leave it alone, since it isn’t your gig
Wipe those cards so you have room
Help finish it: check, then clean
Text them and wait until they reply
questions.explanation: Help out: finish unfinished transfers, following the same check-then-delete process, so nothing gets lost or erased by accident.

questions.prompt: An engineer has run 20 Salmon gigs. Should they still use the Salmon Gig Checklist?
choices: No: the checklist is for beginners
Yes, as a way to double-check
questions.explanation: Even veterans use the checklist. It’s the operational reference and a way to double-check everything.

questions.prompt: A Salmon recital didn’t ask for a livestream. What does the standard workflow say?
choices: Skip the livestream setup, since nobody asked
Stream it publicly anyway, just in case
Practice the livestream, but don’t make it live
Ask the audience whether they want one
questions.explanation: Livestreaming is built into the standard Salmon workflow, so we always practice it. If it wasn’t requested, it doesn’t go live.

questions.prompt: What is the normal workflow for a Salmon gig?
choices: FOH only, with the house PA
Standard A/V recording, livestream built in
Multicam switching with a crew of four
The Standard Gear Kit, carried in
questions.explanation: Standard A/V recording is the normal Salmon workflow, and livestreaming is built into it.

questions.prompt: What crew does a normal Musco gig use?
choices: 1 switcher, 2 camera ops, and 1 score reader
4 camera operators and no switcher at all
1 engineer running everything from the booth
questions.explanation: Musco engineers work as a coordinated crew: a switcher, two camera operators, and a score reader.

questions.prompt: Is multicamera switching a special extra at Musco?
choices: Yes, only for Big Band and Jazz Combo
No: it’s part of the normal Musco workflow
Yes, only when the ensemble requests it
Yes, only for Wassail and Sholund
questions.explanation: Multicamera switching is part of every normal Musco gig.

questions.prompt: At Musco, who calls shots to the camera operators over headset?
choices: Whoever is free in the booth
questions.explanation: The switcher operator runs the live edit, decides what’s on program, and calls shots to the camera operators.

questions.prompt: How many SSDs do you bring to a standard Musco gig?
questions.explanation: Three: one each for the program, the static wide, and the conductor camera.

questions.prompt: What do the three Musco SSDs record?
choices: Audio, video, and a backup copy of both
Camera 1, camera 2, and the H4n backup audio
The program, a spare, and the livestream feed
The program, a static wide ISO, a conductor ISO
questions.explanation: One SSD captures the program (the multicam edit); the other two capture ISOs of the static wide and the conductor camera.

questions.prompt: What is an “ISO” recording?
choices: One camera’s feed, recorded for the whole concert
The live edit that cuts between camera angles
A backup audio file recorded on the H4n
A low-resolution copy made for the livestream
questions.explanation: An ISO is a single camera’s output recorded start to finish. The program is the edit between angles.

questions.prompt: After a Musco concert, an editor wants to replace a bad shot in the multicam edit. Which recording makes that possible?
choices: The program, since it already holds every angle
The ISOs: each holds one camera the whole time
The H4n backup, since it runs the whole concert
Nothing: a live switch can’t be changed later
questions.explanation: The program only contains the angles that were cut to. The ISOs hold their camera for the whole concert, so an editor can cut to them instead.

questions.prompt: An ISO is to the program as ______ is to a stereo mix.
questions.explanation: Like multitrack stems, ISOs keep each source separate. The program, like a stereo mix, has the decisions already made.

questions.prompt: What’s the backup recording at a standard Musco gig?
choices: The CL5 multitrack recording in the basement
A second copy of the program on another SSD
An H4n and an AX100 from the Standard Gear Kit
Two Zoom F8s recording side by side in the booth
questions.explanation: You bring the backup recording yourself: an H4n for audio and an AX100 for video, from the Standard Gear Kit.

questions.prompt: At Big Band and Jazz Combo concerts in Musco, where does the audio team do real-time multitrack live mixing?
choices: On the CL5 in the basement
On the X32 in the booth
On a Zoom F8 in the house
questions.explanation: For the advanced Musco gigs, audio goes down to the basement to mix on the CL5.

questions.prompt: You’re working the Big Band gig at Musco. How should you prepare?
choices: Practice on the CL3 in OH 207
No prep: the CL5 runs itself
questions.explanation: The CL3 in OH 207 is a smaller version of the CL5, so it’s the place to practice.

questions.prompt: What is the Standard Gear Kit?
choices: A portable PA for live sound
questions.explanation: The Standard Gear Kit is the portable rig we carry to gigs where we bring our own recording gear.

questions.prompt: What’s the core setup of the Standard Gear Kit?
choices: Two SM58s into an X32, plus one AX100
A stereo pair into an F8, an H4n backup, two AX100s
One shotgun mic into an H4n, plus three PTZ cameras
A LiveTrak L-20 multitrack, plus one AX100
questions.explanation: A stereo pair of pencil condensers into a Zoom F8, a Zoom H4n Pro for backup audio, and two Sony AX100 cameras.

questions.prompt: Which clean SD cards does the Standard Gear Kit use?
choices: F8: 32 GB · H4n: 8 GB · each AX100: 128 GB
F8: 128 GB · H4n: 32 GB · each AX100: 8 GB
F8: 8 GB · H4n: 128 GB · each AX100: 32 GB
One 128 GB card shared by every device
questions.explanation: A clean 32 GB card for the F8, an 8 GB card for the H4n, and a 128 GB card for each AX100.

questions.prompt: In the Standard Gear Kit, what holds the H4n?
choices: A tripod plate on one of the AX100 tripods
A lighting stand with a ¼-inch screw
Velcro on the telescoping mic stand
Nothing: it sits on a chair in the hall
questions.explanation: The H4n mounts on a lighting stand with a ¼-inch screw.

questions.prompt: In the Standard Gear Kit, where does each stereo-pair mic plug into the F8?
choices: Both into Input 1 with a Y-cable
questions.explanation: Left mic to Input 1, right mic to Input 2. A board feed, if there is one, goes to Inputs 3 and 4.

questions.prompt: If a Standard Gear Kit gig has a board feed, which F8 inputs does it use?
questions.explanation: The main pair is on 1 and 2, the board feed on 3 and 4. Dual Channel Recording copies them to 5–6 and 7–8.

questions.prompt: Dual Channel Recording is on for inputs 1–4, and there’s a board feed. Which tracks hold the lower-level copies of the board feed?
questions.explanation: The board feed is on inputs 3 and 4, so its dual-channel copies land on 7 and 8. The main pair’s copies are on 5 and 6.

questions.prompt: What are the checklist’s starting gains on the F8 for a Standard Gear Kit gig?
choices: About 30 dB on 1–2, about 42 dB on 5–6
About 42 dB on 1–2, about 30 dB on 5–6
0 dB, then turn up during the show
questions.explanation: About 42 dB on the main pair and about 30 dB on the dual-channel copies. They’re starting points; if there’s no time to soundcheck, they’ll be fine.

questions.prompt: How is the F8 powered for a Standard Gear Kit concert?
choices: AC power, with batteries as backup only
Batteries only, so there are no cables
questions.explanation: Use AC power for the concert. Batteries are backup only.

questions.prompt: There’s no chance to hear the loudest passage before the H4n has to start recording. How do you set its level?
choices: As loud as possible, for the best signal
At maximum, then fix it in post
To match the F8’s 42 dB setting
questions.explanation: If you can’t check the loudest passage, set it conservatively. A slightly quiet recording can be fixed; a clipped one can’t.

questions.prompt: On the F8, what should match between the two mics of the stereo pair?
choices: Nothing; set each one by ear
Their pan, both set to center
questions.explanation: Stereo pairs need identical gain so the stereo image isn’t pulled to one side.

questions.prompt: What’s the starting exposure for the AX100s on a Standard Gear Kit gig?
questions.explanation: Start at f/4.0, 3 dB gain, 1/60 shutter, then set exposure under the actual concert lighting.

questions.prompt: What white balance do the two AX100s use?
choices: Auto, set on each camera separately
Whatever looks best on each screen
questions.explanation: Match both cameras to Indoor, or set 3200K manually, so the two angles look the same.

questions.prompt: You set the AX100 exposure under the dim pre-show lights. Then the concert starts and the lights come way up. What happens to the shot?
choices: Nothing, since the settings are locked in
questions.explanation: Pre-show lighting is usually much darker than the performance. Set exposure under concert lighting.

questions.prompt: What do you ask the house staff for before setting the camera exposure?
choices: House lights at half, so the hall is even
Work lights only, so nothing changes later
A spotlight aimed at the camera position
questions.explanation: Ask for concert lighting, the brightest cue used in the performance, so exposure is set for what the show will look like.

questions.prompt: What’s the difference between stereo capture and multitrack capture?
choices: Stereo is one L/R pair; multitrack keeps sources apart
Stereo uses two mics; multitrack uses exactly one mic
Stereo is for video; multitrack is only for audio
No difference: they’re two names for the same thing
questions.explanation: Stereo capture records one left/right picture. Multitrack keeps sources on separate tracks so they can be mixed later.

questions.prompt: What is a board feed?
choices: A backup recording made on an H4n in the hall
A copy of the signal going to the main speakers
A multitrack recording of every input channel
questions.explanation: A board feed is a copy of the mix from the venue’s board, the signal going to the main speakers.

questions.prompt: A film workshop wants to remix the studio musicians later. Which capture fits?
choices: A stereo board feed from the console
Multitrack, on a LiveTrak L-20 or F8
A single H4n placed in the room
questions.explanation: Remixing later needs each source on its own track: a multitrack capture. A board feed or stereo recording has the mix baked in.

questions.prompt: On a Standard Gear Kit gig, when should you ask about a board feed?
choices: Never; the kit doesn’t support one
questions.explanation: If the concert involves electronics, ask for a board feed on arrival. It goes into F8 inputs 3 and 4.

questions.prompt: What is a repo?
choices: A project folder plus its whole history of saved versions
A backup copy on your laptop’s desktop
questions.explanation: A repo (repository) is a project’s files plus every saved version of them. This whole course site is one repo on GitHub.

questions.prompt: Camera-lab, mixer-lab, and the MUS 248 site are each their own repo. Why keep them separate?
choices: Each one does one thing, so a change to one can’t break another
GitHub allows only one website per account
To keep them hidden from each other
questions.explanation: One repo, one thing: each can be changed and fixed on its own without risking the others.

questions.prompt: An activity’s web page, worksheet, and answer key are all built from one Markdown file. Why build them that way?
choices: So the page and the printed worksheet can never disagree
So the worksheet can include the photos
Because only the instructor can read HTML
questions.explanation: One source, one truth: change the file and the page, worksheet, and key all change together.

questions.prompt: What is CLAUDE.md in the course repo?
choices: A file of rules the AI reads before it changes anything
A list of every student’s work
A log of every AI chat
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md holds the repo’s rules for the AI: the repo is public, don’t guess gear details, run the tests, check it in a browser.

questions.prompt: What is a commit?
choices: One saved change, with a short note about what changed
A request for the owner to accept your change
Your own copy of someone else’s repo
questions.explanation: A commit is one save plus a note. The repo’s history keeps every one, so any change can be found and undone.

questions.prompt: Someone commits a door code to a public repo, then deletes the file in the next commit. Is the code safe now?
choices: No: earlier versions stay in the history, where anyone can read them
Yes: deleting the file removes it everywhere
Yes, as long as the commit note says to ignore it
questions.explanation: History keeps every commit, including the one with the code in it. On a public repo, anyone can open that old version.

questions.prompt: Why does every commit get a short note?
choices: So anyone reading the history can tell what changed
The note becomes the page’s title
GitHub Pages only publishes commits with long notes
The note is shown to visitors of the site
questions.explanation: The history is only useful if you can read it: a short note says what each save changed.

questions.prompt: What is a fork on GitHub?
choices: Your own copy of someone else’s repo, under your account
A file of rules for the AI
questions.explanation: A fork is your own copy. You can change it freely, then ask the original’s owner to take your change with a pull request.

questions.prompt: You want to change a repo you don’t own. What do you make first?
choices: A new, empty repo with the same name
questions.explanation: You can’t edit someone else’s repo directly, so you fork it: your own copy to change.

questions.prompt: What does opening a pull request do?
choices: Asks the repo’s owner to bring your change into their repo
Copies the owner’s repo into your account
questions.explanation: A pull request says “here’s my change; please bring it into yours.” Nothing changes until the owner merges it.

questions.prompt: Your pull request is open. Who decides whether your change becomes part of the repo?
choices: The repo’s owner, who can merge it
questions.explanation: A pull request is a request. The owner reviews it, and merging is the owner saying yes.

questions.prompt: On GitHub, what is a merge?
choices: The owner accepting a change into their repo
Making your own copy of a repo
Saving a change with a note
Turning a repo into a website
questions.explanation: Merging brings a pull request’s change into the repo. Fork, commit, pull request, merge: that’s how a change gets in.

questions.prompt: Which file extension usually means a Markdown file?
questions.explanation: Markdown files end in .md, like README.md and every activity’s source file.

questions.prompt: In Markdown, what do the asterisks in **phantom power** do?
questions.explanation: Two asterisks on each side make text bold. Markdown is plain text with a few symbols like that.

questions.prompt: A line in a Markdown file starts with ##. What is it?
questions.explanation: ## starts a heading, ** makes text bold, and - starts a bullet.

questions.prompt: A classmate pastes a chatbot’s answer into Canvas, and it’s full of ## and ** symbols. Why?
choices: The chatbot wrote Markdown, and Canvas showed the raw symbols
Canvas adds those symbols to AI text
questions.explanation: AI tools answer in Markdown. Where Markdown isn’t turned into formatting, you see the symbols themselves.

questions.prompt: Which Markdown line makes a bullet in a list?
questions.explanation: A line starting with a dash and a space is a bullet. ## is a heading, and ** is bold.

questions.prompt: Which best describes a “frontier” AI model?
choices: One of the newest, most capable models from the big AI labs
Any model that’s free to use
A model that runs on your own laptop
questions.explanation: Frontier means the leading edge: the newest, most capable, and most expensive models to run.

questions.prompt: Claude comes in three sizes. Which is the largest?
questions.explanation: Haiku is small, Sonnet is the middle, and Opus is the largest.

questions.prompt: Which Claude model does PantherAI give you?
questions.explanation: PantherAI gives you the highest Sonnet: very good, just not the biggest.

questions.prompt: What is an AI’s context window?
choices: Everything it can “see” at once: your messages, its replies, and what you pasted
The browser window the chat is open in
How many chats you can have open
The websites it has visited today
questions.explanation: The context window is all the AI can see. Anything not in the chat, it doesn’t know about.

questions.prompt: You ask PantherAI to fix a typo on a course web page but don’t paste anything. Why can’t it find the typo?
choices: It only sees what’s in the chat, and the page isn’t in its context window
The page is too new for it to know about
It needs a faster internet connection
It can see the page but isn’t allowed to fix it
questions.explanation: A chatbot can’t see this site, your files, or your screen unless you paste them into the chat.

questions.prompt: A long AI chat keeps ignoring a rule you gave at the start. What’s the most useful fix?
choices: Start a fresh chat with a short summary and the current file
Repeat the rule in ALL CAPS
Paste the whole chat back in
Keep going; it will catch up
questions.explanation: In a long chat, early instructions fade. A fresh chat puts your rules back at the front of the context window.

questions.prompt: Which of these uses the least AI usage, and the least energy?
choices: A clear, specific question in a fresh chat
Turning thinking effort up to the maximum
Pasting your whole project into every message
Switching to the largest model available
questions.explanation: Smaller, clearer asks in fresh chats use less, and they’re usually faster too.

questions.prompt: For a small, clear job, why not just use the biggest model on maximum effort?
choices: More isn’t always better: less is faster, uses less, and does just as well
The biggest model gets small jobs wrong
Maximum effort turns off the context window
questions.explanation: Bigger models and more thinking effort use more. Save them for hard problems.

questions.prompt: Which of these uses more AI usage?
choices: A long chat full of big pastes
A fresh chat with only what’s needed
questions.explanation: Long chats and big pastes mean the AI rereads more every time. Fresh chats with only what’s needed use less.

questions.prompt: Which is an environmental cost of using AI?
choices: Data centers use electricity, and water for cooling
Each chat prints a paper copy
There isn’t one; it all runs on your phone
questions.explanation: Every answer runs in a data center. Bigger models and more thinking use more electricity and water.

questions.prompt: An AI writes a confident summary about a group of people. What’s the best habit?
choices: Check it: AI can repeat the bias in what it learned from, and still sound sure
Trust it, since it sounds confident
Ask it to sound less confident
questions.explanation: AI learns from human writing and picks up its bias, and it sounds just as sure when it’s one-sided. Be most careful about people.

questions.prompt: Which of these is fine to paste into an AI chat?
choices: Your own question about how phantom power works
A classmate’s name and phone number
A recording of a performer, without asking them
questions.explanation: Never paste private things (names, codes, passwords, recordings of people): once it’s sent, you can’t take it back.

questions.prompt: You used AI to help with something you hand in. What does this course ask of you?
choices: Say that you used it, and own the result, mistakes included
Nothing, as long as it’s correct
Blame the AI for any mistakes
Delete the chat so nobody can tell
questions.explanation: Disclose your AI use, like the note at the top of each lecture. You still own what you hand in.

questions.prompt: Which of these is “weightlifting,” where you should do the work yourself?
choices: Practicing a skill you’ll be tested on
Renaming 50 files to match a naming convention
questions.explanation: Weightlifting is when the point is your own growth. Forklifting (routine work that just needs doing) is where AI is probably a good fit.

questions.prompt: Which prompt gets help from AI without cheating?
choices: “Help me understand this without giving me the answers.”
questions.explanation: Use AI to understand, not to skip the thinking, and keep the conversation going for at least three rounds.

questions.prompt: Which prompt makes the best use of a limited prompt budget?
choices: “On my phone the Start button does nothing; on my laptop it works. Fix only that.”
“add more features and fix the bugs”
questions.explanation: One specific change, plus what you saw. Vague prompts spend a turn and get a guess back.

questions.prompt: Your bad webapp looks great in the AI’s reply. When is it done?
choices: When you’ve opened it yourself, on a phone too, and it does what you asked
When the AI says it works
When the code is long enough
questions.explanation: AI sounds equally confident when it’s right and when it’s wrong. It’s done when a person has checked it.

questions.prompt: Your last prompt was “it doesn’t work.” What makes a better one?
choices: Say exactly what you saw, and where: “Tapping Start does nothing on my phone”
Say it louder: “IT STILL DOESN’T WORK”
Ask for three new features at once
Paste the code back with no message
questions.explanation: The AI can’t see your screen. Tell it what happened and where, so it fixes the real problem.

questions.prompt: Why make one change per prompt, then test?
choices: If something breaks, you know which change did it
The AI can only read one sentence
Prompts asking for two changes get rejected
questions.explanation: One change, then test: the same habit as changing one setting at a time on a camera or a mixer.

questions.prompt: What does GitHub Pages do?
choices: Publishes a repo’s files as a website, for free
Makes a private backup of your repo
Writes web pages for you with AI
Prints your repo as a PDF
questions.explanation: GitHub Pages turns a repo into a website: change a file, and a minute later the site changes.

questions.prompt: You turned on Pages, opened your page right away, and got a 404. What should you try first?
choices: Wait a minute, then check the file name letter for letter
Delete the repo and start over
Rename the file to end in .txt
questions.explanation: Pages takes about a minute. After that, a 404 usually means the address and the file name don’t match exactly, capitals included.

questions.prompt: Your page shows your code as plain text instead of running it. What’s the likely problem?
choices: The file name ends in .txt instead of .html
Pages needs a week to start
questions.explanation: The browser only runs it as a web page if the file name ends in .html.

questions.prompt: GitHub says Pages isn’t available for your sandbox repo. What should you check?
choices: That the repo has a long description
That you forked it from someone
That it has a branch named after you
questions.explanation: On a free GitHub account, Pages only publishes public repos.

questions.prompt: You committed a change, but your site still shows the old version. What’s the first thing to do?
choices: Delete the file and add it back
Make the repo private and public again
questions.explanation: Pages takes about a minute to update after a commit. Refresh before changing anything else.

questions.prompt: Your repo is named mus248-sandbox. Where does GitHub Pages publish it?
questions.explanation: A Pages site lives at your username’s github.io address, followed by the repo’s name.

questions.prompt: In your mus248-sandbox, which file is the home page that links to your other two pages?
questions.explanation: index.html is what a visitor sees at your site’s address. It links to bad-webapp.html and gear-dating-profile.html.

questions.prompt: Your group made one bad webapp together. Who publishes it in a mus248-sandbox?
choices: Everyone in the group publishes their own copy
Only the person who typed the prompts
Nobody; it stays in the Playground
questions.explanation: Everyone makes their own mus248-sandbox, and each one has a copy of the group’s bad webapp.

questions.prompt: How do you get your bad webapp’s code out of the Playground?
choices: Open your share link, tap See the code, then select all and copy
Ask PantherAI to email it to you
Take a screenshot of the app
questions.explanation: The share link carries the whole app. See the code shows it, ready to paste into a file in your repo.

questions.prompt: In Markdown, a link is [My app](bad-webapp.html). Which is the same link in HTML?
questions.explanation: HTML spells every part out in tags: <a href="…"> says where the link goes, and the words between the tags are what you click.

questions.prompt: Which one is what the browser reads, with every part spelled out in tags?
questions.explanation: HTML is the browser’s language. Markdown is shorthand, for people.

questions.prompt: Which is a heading written in HTML?
questions.explanation:
In Markdown a heading is # My sandbox. In HTML it’s wrapped in

and

tags.

questions.prompt: Why is Markdown easier to write by hand than HTML?
choices: It uses a few short symbols, like ** for bold, instead of spelling everything out in tags
Markdown can’t have mistakes in it
questions.explanation: Markdown is shorthand: **loud** in Markdown is loud in HTML.

questions.prompt: Who reads your README.md?
choices: People looking at your repo on github.com
questions.explanation: The README shows under the file list on GitHub. Visitors to your site see index.html.

questions.prompt: Someone opens your-username.github.io/mus248-sandbox/. Which file do they see?
choices: The list of files in your repo
questions.explanation: index.html is your site’s home page: what visitors see at its address.

questions.prompt: Your README.md and your index.html both describe your sandbox. Why have both?
choices: Same repo, two audiences: the README is for people on GitHub, index.html for visitors to the site
GitHub needs two copies in case one is deleted
The README is a backup of index.html
index.html is only for the instructor
questions.explanation: People browsing the repo on GitHub see the README (Markdown). People visiting the site see index.html (HTML).

questions.prompt: You’re editing your README on GitHub. What should you check before you commit?
choices: The Preview tab, to see how the Markdown will look
That the README has no headings
questions.explanation: Preview shows the Markdown formatted, so you catch a stray ** before it’s saved.

questions.prompt: What is a branch?
choices: A copy of the files where you try an idea without touching main
Your own copy of someone else’s repo
questions.explanation: A branch is like a duplicate playlist for trying an edit. A fork is a copy of a whole repo under your account.

questions.prompt: You’re fixing one broken step in WTF 248. What’s the right order?
choices: Fork → edit and commit on a new branch → open a pull request
Open a pull request → fork → commit
Commit → open a pull request → fork
questions.explanation: Fork it (your copy), commit the fix on its own branch, then open a pull request so the owner can decide.

questions.prompt: You found two broken steps in WTF 248. How many pull requests should you open?
choices: Two: one fix per branch, and one branch per pull request
One, with both fixes and anything else you noticed
None; committing to your fork is enough
One for each file in the repo
questions.explanation: One fix = one branch = one pull request, so the owner can say yes to each one on its own.

questions.prompt: Which pull request note is the most useful?
choices: “Step 4.3 said to start a fire. Changed it to: turn on the stage lights.”
questions.explanation: A good note says what and why, so the owner can review the fix without hunting for it.

questions.prompt: Which is the best name for a branch that fixes step 4.3?
questions.explanation: Name a branch for what it fixes. main is the branch you’re trying not to touch.

questions.prompt: You forked WTF 248 and committed a fix in your fork. Is the fix in WTF 248 yet?
choices: No: it’s only in your fork until you open a pull request and the owner merges it
Yes: forks stay in sync both ways
Yes, if your commit note is clear
questions.explanation: A fork is your own copy. Your change reaches the original only through a pull request that its owner merges.

questions.prompt: Which is fine to put on your public mus248-sandbox site?
choices: Your GitHub username, or a persona
Your full name and phone number
questions.explanation: Your site is on the public internet. A username or a persona is plenty: no full name, phone, address, or schedule.

questions.prompt: You’re not sure whether something belongs on your public site. What do you do?
choices: Post it, and delete it later if needed
Post it, but only in the README
Post it if the repo is new
questions.explanation: When in doubt, leave it out. Deleting later doesn’t remove it from the repo’s history.

questions.prompt: Your mus248-sandbox repo is public. Who can see it?
choices: Only people with a Chapman login
questions.explanation: Public means public: anyone can find and read your site and every file in the repo.
